abstract_finding: Canonical-pointer paired usable accuracy is 37.1%, compared with 14.3% for native-amount and 40.0% for canonical-amount decoding. Original-input accuracy is 62.9% for native-amount versus 37.1% for canonical-pointer. Evidence-removal refusal accuracy is 0.0% for every base-model arm. Preserving-transform robustness therefore cannot stand in for ordinary accuracy or sensitivity to missing support.
result_interpretation: Canonical-pointer paired usable accuracy is 37.1%, compared with 14.3% for native-amount and 40.0% for canonical-amount decoding. The primary difference is +22.9 percentage points (descriptive 95% interval +5.7 to +40.0). The small-model contrast is +5.7 points (+0.0 to +17.1). These are pilot estimates on reused companies, not external validation. Canonical-amount matches or exceeds canonical-pointer on the primary condition; this experiment does not establish an additional benefit from pointer output. Original-input accuracy is 62.9% for native-amount versus 37.1% for canonical-pointer. Evidence-removal refusal accuracy is 0.0% for every base-model arm. Preserving-transform robustness therefore cannot stand in for ordinary accuracy or sensitivity to missing support.
failure_example: A recorded regression is adi-numeric-01 with base/native_amount. Its original answer is correct, but after synthetic unit rescaling the model outputs `12305.539`; the required value remains 12305539 USD thousands. The report includes every such scale regression, not just this illustration.
